title: Jupiter Has Its Own, Busier Way of Blocking the Solar Wind
summary:
NASA's Juno spacecraft has found that Jupiter, the solar system's largest planet, withstands the Sun's particle stream with a much more complex system of plasma waves and shock regions than Earth uses, in research led by scientists at the University of Iowa.

The Sun continuously releases a stream of electrically charged particles called the solar wind. When the solar wind approaches a planet with a magnetic field, it meets a boundary known as the bow shock.

At Earth, this boundary slows and heats incoming particles and redirects much of the solar wind around the planet. Without it, more harmful particles could reach the atmosphere. Jupiter also has a bow shock, but its enormous size, powerful magnetic field and gaseous makeup make it especially interesting to study.

Using measurements from Juno, researchers discovered that Jupiter relies on plasma waves with multiple frequencies to slow and heat incoming solar particles. These different frequencies, known as harmonics, create a more elaborate wave pattern than the one typically observed at Earth. It works a bit like music: several notes together sound richer than one note, and waves with multiple frequencies interact with particles in more complex ways, heating more of them and slowing them down. Earth's bow shock, by comparison, primarily uses waves concentrated around a single frequency.

Jupiter also has an extra line of defense. Before incoming particles reach the main bow shock, they can encounter smaller shock structures called shocklets, which help slow the solar wind first. Earth generally relies on its main bow shock alone. Earth does not need these extra steps because the impact is not as powerful, said Bill Kurth, an Iowa research scientist on the Juno mission since its 2011 launch.

Beyond Jupiter, the results could help scientists understand some of the most powerful events in the universe, including the extreme shock waves associated with exploding stars.
why_it_matters: Learning how Jupiter tames a much stronger solar wind helps scientists protect spacecraft and understand the violent shock waves around exploding stars.

Hubble

questions.question: What is the solar wind?
options: A storm of dust around Mars
A stream of electrically charged particles continuously released by the Sun
Light reflected off the Moon
Heat rising from Earth's core
questions.correct_answer: A stream of electrically charged particles continuously released by the Sun

questions.question: What does Earth's bow shock do to incoming solar particles?
options: It speeds them up toward the ground
It turns them into visible light
It traps them in Earth's oceans
It slows and heats them and redirects much of the solar wind around the planet
questions.correct_answer: It slows and heats them and redirects much of the solar wind around the planet

questions.question: How does Jupiter's wave pattern differ from Earth's?
options: Earth uses shocklets and Jupiter does not
Both planets use exactly the same wave pattern
Jupiter has no plasma waves at all
Jupiter uses plasma waves with multiple frequencies, while Earth's waves are concentrated around a single frequency
questions.correct_answer: Jupiter uses plasma waves with multiple frequencies, while Earth's waves are concentrated around a single frequency

questions.question: What are shocklets?
options: Craters on Jupiter's surface
Bursts of light from the Sun
Smaller shock structures that slow the solar wind before it reaches the main bow shock
Tiny moons orbiting Jupiter
questions.correct_answer: Smaller shock structures that slow the solar wind before it reaches the main bow shock

questions.question: Why does Earth generally not need shocklets, according to Bill Kurth?
options: Because Earth's bow shock is larger than Jupiter's
Because Earth has no magnetic field
Because the solar wind never reaches Earth
Because the impact on Earth is not as powerful
questions.correct_answer: Because the impact on Earth is not as powerful

background_read: The Sun constantly sends out a stream of electrically charged particles, and this stream is called the solar wind.
Many planets have a magnetic field, an invisible force around the planet that can push back against charged particles from space.
When the solar wind runs into a planet's magnetic field, it forms a boundary that slows and heats the particles and steers most of them around the planet.
Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system, and its great size and strong magnetic field make its boundary with the solar wind especially powerful and interesting to study.
